column1: A neutral carbon atom commonly forms four bonds in closed-shell organic molecules.|T|Four shared pairs complete carbon’s usual octet in these structures.
A carbon atom with four single bonds is typically tetrahedral.|T|The four bonding directions are approximately 109.5 degrees apart.
An sp² carbon has a trigonal-planar arrangement of its three sigma-bond directions.|T|An unhybridized p orbital remains available for pi bonding.
A carbon-carbon triple bond contains three sigma bonds.|F|It contains one sigma bond and two pi bonds.
Sigma bonding can arise from end-to-end orbital overlap.|T|Electron density lies along the line connecting the nuclei.
A pi bond permits unrestricted rotation without losing orbital overlap.|F|Rotating the bonded atoms disrupts sideways p-orbital overlap.
A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons not assigned to an ordinary covalent bond.|T|Lone pairs affect charge, geometry, and chemical reactivity.
The octet rule has no exceptions for any element.|F|Electron-deficient, odd-electron, and some heavier-element structures do not follow a simple octet description.

Shorter carbon-carbon bonds generally correspond to higher bond order among single, double, and triple bonds.|T|Greater shared bonding concentrates electron density between the nuclei and usually shortens the bond.
Electronegativity describes an atom’s attraction for shared electrons.|T|Different electronegativities create unequal electron sharing in a bond.
Formal charge and partial charge are always numerically identical.|F|Formal charge is bookkeeping; partial charge describes unequal actual electron distribution.
Resonance contributors are separate molecules rapidly converting into one another.|F|They are alternative drawings of one delocalized electronic structure.
A resonance contributor can move atoms while retaining its identity as a resonance form.|F|Only electrons move between contributors; atomic connectivity remains fixed.
A Lewis base donates an electron pair.|T|The pair can form a bond to a Lewis acid.
A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.|T|It need not donate a proton to act as a Lewis acid.
A lower pKa corresponds to a stronger acid under the same conditions.|T|It means a larger acid-dissociation constant and greater proton-donation tendency.
A more stable conjugate base generally corresponds to a stronger parent acid.|T|Stabilizing the deprotonated form favors proton loss.
Acid-base equilibrium generally favors the side containing the stronger acid.|F|It usually favors the weaker acid and weaker base when comparing the relevant conjugate pairs.
An acyclic saturated alkane with n carbons has formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.|T|A connected open-chain carbon skeleton with only single bonds has that hydrogen count.
Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity.|T|The atoms connect in different sequences or branching patterns.
Rotation about a carbon-carbon single bond creates different conformations.|T|The connectivity stays the same while spatial arrangement changes.
Staggered ethane is higher in energy than eclipsed ethane.|F|Eclipsing interactions create a torsional energy cost, so the staggered conformation is lower.
A Newman projection views a molecule along a bond axis.|T|It shows relative orientations of substituents on the near and far atoms.
Anti butane places its two methyl groups opposite each other in a staggered view.|T|Their dihedral angle is 180 degrees, minimizing their close contact.
Gauche and anti butane have different molecular formulas.|F|They are conformations of the same molecule and share both formula and connectivity.
The parent name of an alkane is chosen using an appropriate longest continuous carbon chain.|T|The nomenclature rules then identify substituents and assign positions.
Branching can affect an alkane’s boiling point even when molecular formula is unchanged.|T|Shape changes intermolecular contact and the strength of cumulative dispersion interactions.
Cycloalkanes contain at least one ring of carbon atoms.|T|A ring joins parts of the carbon skeleton that would otherwise be an open chain.
Every cycloalkane is planar.|F|Many rings pucker to reduce angle and torsional strain.
Cyclopropane has substantial angle strain.|T|Its small ring forces bond directions far from ideal tetrahedral geometry.
The chair conformation of cyclohexane largely avoids eclipsing interactions.|T|Its bonds are approximately staggered with near-tetrahedral angles.
A cyclohexane ring flip interchanges axial and equatorial positions.|T|Substituents retain their up or down direction while switching axial/equatorial roles.
A ring flip changes cis substituents into trans substituents.|F|It changes conformation but preserves their relative up/down configuration.
A bulky substituent on cyclohexane generally prefers an equatorial position.|T|This reduces unfavorable 1,3-diaxial interactions.
Cis substituents on a ring lie on the same side of the ring framework.|T|Both are up or both are down in the usual depiction.
Angle strain and torsional strain describe the same physical feature.|F|Angle strain concerns bond-angle distortion; torsional strain concerns eclipsing or related bond alignment.
A chiral molecule is not superimposable on its mirror image.|T|Its two mirror-related forms have distinct three-dimensional handedness.
A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups is a stereogenic center.|T|Exchanging two groups changes its configuration when the full substituent identities are different.
Every molecule containing stereocenters is chiral.|F|An internal symmetry element can make a meso compound achiral despite having stereocenters.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images.|T|They have opposite configurations at all corresponding stereogenic centers in the usual comparison.
Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.|T|They can differ at some, but not all, stereogenic elements.
An R designation automatically means a compound rotates polarized light clockwise.|F|R/S describes absolute configuration; optical rotation direction must be determined independently.
A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers.|T|Their equal opposite optical rotations cancel in an ordinary achiral measurement environment.
CIP priorities start by comparing atomic numbers of directly attached atoms.|T|Higher atomic number has higher priority; tied atoms require examining the next layer.
Rotating a molecule in space necessarily changes its R or S configuration.|F|Physical rotation preserves configuration; swapping substituents is a different operation.
An electron-pair curved arrow begins at an electron source.|T|It starts at a lone pair or bond and points to the destination of that electron pair.
A full curved arrow represents the movement of an atomic nucleus.|F|It tracks electrons; atoms follow the resulting changes in bonding.
A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor in a reaction.|T|It attacks an electron-poor site using available electron density.
An electrophile accepts electron density.|T|Its electron deficiency or polar bonding makes it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.
Homolytic bond cleavage gives one electron to each fragment.|T|It creates radicals rather than assigning the whole pair to one side.
Heterolytic cleavage divides the two bond electrons equally.|F|One fragment receives both electrons, commonly producing ions.
A transition state is a stable intermediate that can usually be isolated.|F|It is an energy maximum along the reaction path, not a local-energy-minimum species.
An exergonic reaction necessarily has a negligible activation barrier.|F|Overall energy favorability does not determine how large the barrier is.
A catalyst changes the mechanism and rate without changing the overall equilibrium constant.|T|It supplies an alternative path while preserving the initial and final thermodynamic states.
A carbon-carbon double bond contains one sigma bond and one pi bond.|T|The pi component comes from sideways overlap of neighboring p orbitals.
Each alkene carbon is usually approximately trigonal planar.|T|Its three sigma-bond directions are associated with sp² hybridization.
E/Z stereochemistry requires two different substituents on each double-bond carbon.|T|Without that distinction, exchanging sides cannot generate distinct E and Z forms.
Z means the higher-priority groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.|F|Z places them on the same side; E places them on opposite sides.
Hydrogen deficiency can indicate rings or pi bonds.|T|A ring or double bond reduces the saturated acyclic hydrogen count by two; a triple bond reduces it by four.
More substituted simple alkenes are often more stable than less substituted ones.|T|Alkyl substitution can stabilize the double bond, although steric and structural factors also matter.
An electrophile can attack an alkene’s electron-rich pi bond.|T|The pi electrons can form a new sigma bond to the electrophile.
A carbocation has a fully occupied octet at its positively charged carbon in the ordinary model.|F|The typical carbocation has an empty p orbital and an incomplete octet.
Carbocation rearrangement can occur during some alkene addition reactions.|T|A hydride or alkyl shift can form a more stable carbocation before capture.
Catalytic hydrogenation adds hydrogen across an alkene double bond.|T|The pi bond is replaced by two new carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds.
Hydrogenation on a metal surface normally gives syn addition.|T|The two hydrogens are delivered from the same face of the adsorbed alkene.

Hydroboration–oxidation gives an alcohol with the hydroxyl group on the less substituted alkene carbon in the usual case.|T|The sequence produces anti-Markovnikov hydration without a free carbocation intermediate.
Hydroboration–oxidation is normally anti addition of hydrogen and hydroxyl.|F|The overall addition is syn, with hydrogen and hydroxyl delivered to the same face.
Bromination of a simple alkene commonly proceeds through a bromonium ion.|T|The bridged intermediate explains the usual anti addition of bromine.
Acid-catalyzed hydration can involve carbocation rearrangement.|T|A sufficiently long-lived carbocation may rearrange before water attacks.
Ozonolysis can cleave an alkene into carbonyl-containing fragments.|T|The products depend on substitution and the workup conditions.
Epoxidation adds one oxygen across an alkene to form a three-membered ring.|T|The two original alkene carbons both bond to the transferred oxygen.
All alkene addition reactions have the same regiochemistry and stereochemistry.|F|Different reagents and mechanisms give different orientation and face-selectivity patterns.
An alkyne contains a carbon-carbon triple bond.|T|Its triple bond contains one sigma and two pi components.
The two carbon centers of a simple alkyne are approximately linear.|T|Their sp-hybridized sigma directions are separated by about 180 degrees.
A terminal alkyne is more acidic than a typical alkane.|T|Its conjugate base places the lone pair in an orbital with greater s character.
A weak base such as hydroxide fully deprotonates a typical terminal alkyne in water.|F|The alkyne is much less acidic than water, so a much stronger base is generally required.
An acetylide anion can form a carbon-carbon bond by suitable SN2 alkylation.|T|It attacks an unhindered electrophilic carbon and displaces a leaving group.
A tertiary alkyl halide is an ideal substrate for acetylide SN2 alkylation.|F|Steric hindrance blocks SN2 and strong-base elimination commonly competes.
Lindlar-catalyzed partial hydrogenation gives a cis alkene from a suitable internal alkyne.|T|The poisoned catalyst stops at the alkene and delivers hydrogen syn.
Dissolving-metal reduction of a suitable internal alkyne gives mainly a trans alkene.|T|Its stepwise electron/proton sequence favors anti overall hydrogen addition.
An enol and its keto tautomer differ only by electron placement with identical atom positions.|F|Tautomerization moves a proton and changes a pi bond; it is not merely resonance.
An organohalide contains a carbon-halogen bond.|T|The halogen can be fluorine, chlorine, bromine, or iodine.
The carbon-halogen bond in a typical alkyl halide is polarized toward carbon.|F|The halogen is usually more electronegative, leaving carbon partly positive.
A primary alkyl halide has its halogen-bearing carbon attached to one other carbon.|T|Classification concerns the substitution of that particular carbon, not total molecule size.
Radical halogenation can involve initiation, propagation, and termination steps.|T|The chain is sustained by radical regeneration during propagation.
A radical contains an unpaired electron.|T|Its electron count differs from a paired-electron closed-shell species.
Allylic radicals can be stabilized by resonance.|T|The unpaired electron can be delocalized over the adjacent pi system.
Grignard reagents can survive unchanged in ordinary water.|F|Water protonates the carbon-magnesium reagent and destroys its intended carbon nucleophilicity.
A carbon-magnesium bond makes carbon strongly nucleophilic and basic.|T|Its polarity gives carbon substantial carbanion-like character.
All organohalides have identical reactivity regardless of carbon hybridization and substitution.|F|Bond environment and steric accessibility strongly affect their reactions.
An SN2 reaction occurs in one concerted substitution step.|T|Bond formation and leaving-group departure occur together without a carbocation intermediate.
SN2 normally gives inversion at a stereogenic reacting carbon.|T|Backside attack changes the spatial arrangement at that center.
A tertiary alkyl halide usually reacts fastest by SN2.|F|Steric crowding makes backside attack difficult; less substituted centers are generally more accessible.
An SN1 mechanism typically involves carbocation formation.|T|Leaving-group departure precedes nucleophile capture in the standard mechanism.
Increasing nucleophile concentration changes the ideal SN1 rate law directly.|F|The rate-determining ionization is first order in substrate, not nucleophile.
E2 elimination is concerted.|T|A base removes a proton as the leaving group departs and the pi bond forms.
An anti-periplanar arrangement is commonly favored for E2 elimination.|T|It aligns the breaking bonds for effective formation of the new pi bond.
E1 elimination can undergo carbocation rearrangement.|T|The intermediate carbocation can rearrange before proton loss.
A strong bulky base can favor a less substituted alkene in elimination.|T|Steric access can favor removal of a less hindered beta hydrogen.
Mass spectrometry measures ions according to mass-to-charge ratio.|T|The detected signal positions reflect m/z rather than neutral molecular mass alone.
The molecular ion is always the most intense peak.|F|Fragment ions can be more abundant; the base peak is defined by maximum intensity.
An isotope pattern can help reveal chlorine or bromine in a compound.|T|Their characteristic isotope abundances create informative peak patterns.
An IR absorption requires a vibrational change that changes molecular dipole moment.|T|This selection rule explains why some vibrations absorb weakly or not at all.
Higher IR wavenumber corresponds to lower vibrational frequency.|F|Wavenumber and frequency are directly proportional through the speed of light.
An alcohol O–H stretch is often broad.|T|Hydrogen bonding spreads the absorption across a range of vibrational environments.
A carbonyl group commonly gives a strong IR absorption in its characteristic region.|T|Its stretching vibration strongly changes dipole moment.
One IR peak uniquely determines an entire molecular structure in every case.|F|Functional-group clues must be combined with other bands and complementary structural information.
A mass-spectrum fragment can provide information about molecular connectivity.|T|Favored bond cleavages and stable ion structures help explain the fragments.
Chemically equivalent protons generally contribute to the same NMR signal.|T|Equivalent environments have matching chemical shifts under the relevant measurement conditions.
A proton NMR integration estimates the relative number of contributing hydrogens.|T|Peak areas, not just peak heights, are compared.
More shielded protons generally resonate upfield at smaller chemical shift.|T|Shielding reduces the effective magnetic field experienced by the nucleus.
Chemical shift in ppm changes proportionally with spectrometer field strength.|F|The ppm scale normalizes the frequency difference by the operating frequency.
The simple n + 1 splitting rule applies without exceptions to every spectrum.|F|It assumes a suitable first-order coupling pattern, often involving equivalent neighboring protons.
Exchangeable O–H protons can show variable shifts and broadening.|T|Hydrogen bonding and exchange depend on solvent, concentration, and other conditions.
Carbon-13 NMR can help count distinct carbon environments.|T|Symmetry and equivalence can reduce the number of observed resonances.
Two enantiomers normally give different NMR spectra in an achiral solvent.|F|They ordinarily have identical spectra under achiral conditions; a chiral environment can distinguish them.
NMR signals arise from nuclear spin energy differences in a magnetic field.|T|Radiofrequency absorption probes transitions between the relevant spin states.
Conjugated double bonds are separated by one single bond.|T|Adjacent p orbitals can overlap continuously across the alternating bonding pattern.
Conjugation can stabilize a molecule through electron delocalization.|T|Spreading pi electron density changes orbital energies and lowers overall energy in many such systems.
An isolated diene has the same continuous p-orbital overlap as a conjugated diene.|F|An interruption prevents the same extended conjugation.
Addition to a conjugated diene can give both 1,2 and 1,4 products.|T|A delocalized intermediate allows bond formation at more than one position.
The kinetic product is defined as the most thermodynamically stable product.|F|It is the product formed through the faster pathway under kinetic control.
Thermodynamic control favors the more stable product when equilibration is possible.|T|Reversible conditions allow the product distribution to approach equilibrium.
A Diels–Alder reaction combines a conjugated diene with a dienophile.|T|The cycloaddition forms a six-membered ring with a remaining double bond.
A diene must be able to adopt an s-cis arrangement for a normal Diels–Alder reaction.|T|The termini must be positioned to form the two new sigma bonds.
Increasing conjugation often shifts absorption toward longer UV-visible wavelengths.|T|The energy gap between relevant orbitals commonly decreases with increased conjugation.
Benzene has equal carbon-carbon bond lengths in its equilibrium structure.|T|Its delocalized pi system does not alternate ordinary isolated single and double bond lengths.
Every cyclic molecule is aromatic.|F|Aromaticity additionally requires suitable conjugation, geometry, and electron count.
A planar fully conjugated monocyclic system with 4n + 2 pi electrons satisfies Hückel’s aromaticity rule.|T|That count fills the bonding pi orbitals in the standard closed-shell model.
A planar fully conjugated 4n-pi-electron ring is normally antiaromatic.|T|Its electronic arrangement is destabilized relative to suitable noncyclic references.
A nonplanar ring must be classified as antiaromatic solely because it has 4n pi electrons.|F|Loss of continuous planar conjugation can make it nonaromatic instead.
The cyclopentadienyl anion can be aromatic.|T|Its five-membered conjugated ring has six pi electrons, including the lone-pair contribution.
Pyridine’s nitrogen lone pair is part of its six-electron aromatic pi system.|F|The lone pair lies in an in-plane orbital; a different nitrogen orbital contributes to the pi system.
Pyrrole’s nitrogen lone pair contributes two electrons to the aromatic pi system.|T|Its single nitrogen lone pair participates in completing the six-pi-electron system.

Aromatic stabilization helps explain benzene’s preference for substitution rather than ordinary alkene addition.|T|Substitution can restore the aromatic system, whereas addition would remove that stabilization.
Electrophilic aromatic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen while restoring aromaticity.|T|Electrophilic attack is followed by proton loss to re-form the aromatic pi system.
The sigma-complex intermediate in electrophilic aromatic substitution retains full aromaticity.|F|One ring carbon becomes tetrahedral, interrupting the continuous aromatic pi system temporarily.
An electron-donating substituent often activates benzene toward electrophilic substitution.|T|Donation stabilizes electron-deficient intermediates and can lower the reaction barrier.
A strongly electron-withdrawing nitro group generally directs further substitution meta.|T|Ortho and para attack create especially unfavorable resonance contributors for the intermediate.
Halogens are generally activating ortho/para directors.|F|They direct ortho/para but deactivate the ring overall through strong inductive withdrawal.
A Friedel–Crafts alkylation can undergo carbocation rearrangement.|T|The electrophilic carbon species may rearrange before attaching to the ring.
Friedel–Crafts acylation introduces an acyl group onto the aromatic ring.|T|The product is an aryl ketone after the usual workup.
Friedel–Crafts reactions work equally well on strongly deactivated nitrobenzene.|F|Strong deactivation prevents the usual reaction under standard Friedel–Crafts conditions.
Substituent effects help plan the order of reactions in aromatic synthesis.|T|Earlier groups can activate, deactivate, and direct where later groups are introduced.
An alcohol contains an O–H group attached to a saturated carbon in the usual functional-group classification.|T|Phenols instead have the O–H group directly attached to an aromatic ring.
Alcohols can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.|T|The O–H bond donates, while oxygen lone pairs accept hydrogen bonds.
Phenol is generally more acidic than a typical aliphatic alcohol.|T|Its conjugate base is stabilized by resonance in the aromatic framework.
A tertiary alcohol can be oxidized to a ketone without breaking any carbon-carbon bonds.|F|The hydroxyl-bearing carbon lacks the needed hydrogen; ordinary oxidation does not simply give a ketone.
A secondary alcohol can be oxidized to a ketone.|T|Removing hydrogen from oxygen and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon creates the carbonyl.
A primary alcohol may be oxidized to an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid depending on conditions.|T|The reagent and water availability influence whether oxidation stops or continues.
Hydroxide is an excellent leaving group from an unactivated alcohol.|F|It is a poor leaving group; protonation or conversion to a better leaving group facilitates substitution.
Acid-catalyzed alcohol dehydration can form an alkene.|T|Loss of water and a neighboring proton creates the pi bond.
An alkoxide is the conjugate base of an alcohol.|T|Removing the hydroxyl proton leaves a negatively charged oxygen.
An ether has an oxygen bonded to two carbon groups.|T|It has no O–H bond unless another functional group is present elsewhere.
Ordinary ethers can accept hydrogen bonds from water.|T|Their oxygen lone pairs can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.
An ether with no O–H bond can donate hydrogen bonds in the same way an alcohol does.|F|It lacks the directly bonded hydroxyl hydrogen needed for that donor role.
An epoxide is a three-membered cyclic ether.|T|Its small ring is strained and susceptible to ring-opening reactions.
Under basic conditions, a simple unsymmetrical epoxide is usually attacked at the less substituted carbon.|T|Backside SN2-like attack favors the less hindered site.

Acid-catalyzed epoxide opening requires considering both charge development and steric accessibility.|T|Protonation activates the ring and changes regioselectivity compared with unprotonated basic opening.
Williamson ether synthesis commonly uses an alkoxide and a suitable primary alkyl halide.|T|An SN2 displacement forms the carbon-oxygen bond efficiently with limited steric hindrance.
Thiols contain an S–H group.|T|They are sulfur analogues of alcohols but differ in acidity and other properties.
Oxidation of two thiols can form a disulfide bond.|T|The resulting S–S linkage is important in both small molecules and protein structure.
A carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.|T|The polarized carbon-oxygen bond leaves carbon electron-poor relative to oxygen.
An aldehyde has at least one hydrogen attached directly to the carbonyl carbon.|T|A ketone instead has two carbon substituents there.
Nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl initially changes its carbon from planar toward tetrahedral geometry.|T|A new sigma bond forms as pi electrons shift toward oxygen.
Ketones are generally more reactive than comparable aldehydes toward simple nucleophilic addition.|F|Aldehydes are typically less hindered and less electron-donated, making them more reactive.
Hydride reduction of a ketone gives a secondary alcohol after workup.|T|The carbonyl carbon gains hydrogen and the oxygen is protonated.
A primary amine can form an imine with an aldehyde or ketone under suitable conditions.|T|Addition followed by dehydration replaces the carbonyl oxygen with a nitrogen-containing double bond.
Acetal formation is typically acid-catalyzed.|T|Acid helps activate the carbonyl and enables loss of water during the substitution sequence.
Acetals are commonly used as carbonyl protecting groups under basic conditions.|T|They resist many basic reactions but can be hydrolyzed under aqueous acid.
A carbonyl-addition product must retain the original carbon-oxygen double bond.|F|Addition converts the pi bond into new single-bond connectivity unless later elimination restores it.
A carboxyl group contains a carbonyl and hydroxyl on the same carbon.|T|The linked groups give carboxylic acids their characteristic acidity and reactivity.
A carboxylate anion has resonance-delocalized negative charge over two oxygens.|T|The two main contributors explain the equivalent carbon-oxygen bonding in a symmetric environment.
Electron-withdrawing substituents can increase carboxylic-acid acidity.|T|They stabilize the conjugate base through inductive or resonance effects when positioned appropriately.
A carboxylic acid is generally less acidic than an ordinary alcohol.|F|Its resonance-stabilized conjugate base makes it considerably more acidic.
A nitrile contains a carbon-nitrogen triple bond.|T|The nitrile carbon is bonded to nitrogen through one sigma and two pi bonds.
Hydrolysis of a nitrile can produce a carboxylic acid or carboxylate depending on conditions.|T|The nitrile nitrogen is replaced through a sequence involving addition and an amide intermediate.
Reducing a nitrile can give a primary amine.|T|The carbon-nitrogen triple bond is converted to a single bond with added hydrogens.
A Grignard reagent can add carbon dioxide to produce a carboxylate before acidic workup.|T|The nucleophilic carbon forms a new carbon-carbon bond to carbon dioxide’s carbon.
Carboxylic acids never form hydrogen bonds.|F|They can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, often forming associated dimers in suitable media.
Nucleophilic acyl substitution replaces a group attached to a carbonyl carbon.|T|Addition to the carbonyl is followed by elimination that restores the carbonyl.
A tetrahedral intermediate can occur in nucleophilic acyl substitution.|T|The carbonyl pi bond temporarily becomes a single bond during nucleophilic addition.
Acid chlorides are generally more reactive toward acyl substitution than amides.|T|Chloride is a better leaving group and amide resonance strongly stabilizes the starting amide.
Amides have nitrogen lone-pair delocalization into the carbonyl system.|T|This resonance reduces carbonyl electrophilicity and gives the carbon-nitrogen bond partial double-bond character.
Fischer esterification combines a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under acid catalysis.|T|It is an equilibrium process that forms an ester and water.
Removing water can help drive an equilibrium esterification toward ester.|T|Removing a product shifts the equilibrium in the product-forming direction.
Saponification is base-promoted ester hydrolysis.|T|The carboxylate product helps drive the reaction and is protonated only if an acid workup follows.
An ester and an ether are the same functional group.|F|An ester has an oxygen attached to a carbonyl carbon; an ether does not require a carbonyl.
Reduction of an amide by a strong hydride reagent can give an amine.|T|The carbonyl oxygen is removed while the carbon-nitrogen connectivity is retained.
An alpha carbon is adjacent to a carbonyl carbon.|T|Hydrogens on that neighboring carbon can participate in enol and enolate chemistry.
An enolate can delocalize negative charge between oxygen and an alpha carbon.|T|Its resonance contributors explain both oxygen and carbon nucleophilicity.
Every carbonyl compound has alpha hydrogens.|F|Some structures have no hydrogen on any adjacent carbon, preventing ordinary enolization there.
Keto-enol tautomerization moves a proton and a pi bond.|T|The two forms are constitutional isomers connected by proton-transfer chemistry, not just resonance drawings.
Alpha hydrogens of a ketone are generally more acidic than ordinary alkane hydrogens.|T|Deprotonation gives a resonance-stabilized enolate.
A kinetic enolate is selected by the fastest deprotonation pathway under suitable conditions.|T|Bulky strong base and low temperature can favor access to a less hindered alpha position.
The thermodynamic enolate is defined solely as whichever one forms fastest.|F|It is the more stable enolate favored when equilibration is possible.
Enolate alkylation can form a new carbon-carbon bond.|T|The carbon nucleophile displaces a suitable leaving group, often through SN2.
A tertiary alkyl halide is usually a good SN2 partner for enolate alkylation.|F|Steric hindrance and elimination make it unsuitable for the usual clean SN2 route.
An aldol addition joins an enolate donor with a carbonyl acceptor.|T|The donor’s alpha carbon forms a bond to the acceptor’s carbonyl carbon.
A simple aldol addition product contains a beta-hydroxy carbonyl group.|T|The original donor carbonyl remains and the acceptor oxygen becomes the hydroxyl.
Aldol condensation commonly includes dehydration after addition.|T|Loss of water can produce a conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound.
Every carbonyl partner in a crossed aldol reaction must have alpha hydrogens.|F|Only the enolate donor needs them; an acceptor without alpha hydrogens can improve selectivity.
An intramolecular aldol reaction can form a ring.|T|The donor and acceptor groups lie within the same molecule.
Claisen condensation involves ester enolate attack on an ester carbonyl.|T|Acyl substitution forms a beta-keto ester in the common self-condensation case.
A Claisen condensation is identical to an aldol addition with no leaving-group loss.|F|The ester acceptor expels an alkoxide during acyl substitution.
A Michael addition is conjugate addition to an activated unsaturated system.|T|A nucleophile adds at the beta position of an alpha,beta-unsaturated acceptor in the usual case.
Robinson annulation combines Michael addition and an intramolecular aldol sequence.|T|The sequence can build a six-membered ring containing an enone.
Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia.|T|Carbon groups replace one, two, or three ammonia hydrogens in primary, secondary, or tertiary amines.
A primary amine’s nitrogen is bonded to one carbon group.|T|Its remaining ordinary single bonds are to two hydrogens in the neutral form.
The nitrogen lone pair commonly makes an amine basic.|T|It can accept a proton to form an ammonium ion.
An amide nitrogen is usually as basic as a comparable alkylamine nitrogen.|F|Delocalization into the carbonyl reduces availability of the amide nitrogen lone pair.
Aniline’s lone pair can interact with the aromatic ring.|T|Delocalization makes it less available for protonation than in many aliphatic amines.
A quaternary ammonium nitrogen has four carbon substituents and a positive formal charge.|T|It has four sigma bonds and no neutral-amine lone pair.
Pyridine contains a nitrogen atom in an aromatic six-membered ring.|T|Its lone pair is outside the aromatic pi electron set and can accept a proton.
Ordinary pyramidal amines can invert their nitrogen geometry rapidly.|T|This inversion often prevents isolation of nitrogen enantiomers unless structural constraints block it.
Amine salts can be more water-soluble than their neutral parent amines.|T|The ionic form interacts strongly with water, although the full structure also affects solubility.
A monosaccharide cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller carbohydrates.|T|It is a single sugar unit rather than a linked assembly of sugar units.
An aldose contains an aldehyde in its open-chain form.|T|A ketose instead contains a ketone in its open-chain form.
D and L sugar labels directly specify the sign of optical rotation.|F|They describe configuration relative to a reference system, not the measured rotation direction.
A sugar’s cyclic hemiacetal can form by intramolecular alcohol addition to its carbonyl.|T|This creates a new anomeric stereocenter when the two possible configurations are distinct.
Anomers differ in configuration at the anomeric carbon.|T|Other stereocenters stay the same in the corresponding pair.
Mutarotation involves interconversion of anomers through ring opening and reclosing.|T|The changing anomer ratio changes the measured optical rotation.
A glycosidic bond can link sugar units.|T|It involves an anomeric center and a heteroatom linkage to another group.
Every disaccharide is a reducing sugar.|F|If both anomeric centers are locked in the linkage, no free reducing end remains.
Cellulose and starch have identical glycosidic stereochemistry.|F|Their differing linkage configurations produce major differences in structure and biological processing.
A typical alpha-amino acid has amino and carboxyl groups attached to the same alpha carbon.|T|Its side chain supplies the distinguishing chemical properties.
Every standard protein amino acid has a chiral alpha carbon.|F|Glycine has two hydrogens on its alpha carbon and is achiral there.
A zwitterion contains both positive and negative formal charges in the same molecule.|T|An amino acid can contain an ammonium group and a carboxylate simultaneously.
A peptide bond is an amide linkage.|T|It joins the carboxyl-derived carbon of one residue to the amino nitrogen of another.
Peptide bonds rotate freely like ordinary carbon-carbon single bonds.|F|Amide resonance gives partial double-bond character and restricts rotation.
Protein primary structure is the amino-acid sequence.|T|It specifies residue order rather than the full folded three-dimensional shape.
Alpha helices and beta sheets are examples of secondary structure.|T|Their recurring backbone arrangements are stabilized by hydrogen bonding.
Denaturation necessarily breaks every peptide bond.|F|It mainly disrupts higher-order structure; the primary chain can remain intact.
Disulfide bonds can link cysteine side chains.|T|Oxidation of two thiol groups forms an S–S linkage that can stabilize structure.
Triacylglycerols contain three fatty-acid residues esterified to glycerol.|T|All three glycerol hydroxyl groups are converted to ester linkages.
A saturated fatty acid contains a carbon-carbon double bond by definition.|F|Its hydrocarbon chain has no carbon-carbon double bonds.
A cis double bond can introduce a bend in a fatty-acid chain.|T|The bend disrupts close packing relative to an otherwise similar straight saturated chain.
Hydrolyzing a triacylglycerol can release glycerol and fatty acids or their salts.|T|The exact acid or carboxylate products depend on hydrolysis conditions.
Phospholipids can have both a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.|T|This amphiphilic character promotes bilayer formation in water.
All lipids have the same repeating polymer backbone.|F|Lipids are a diverse group defined largely by solubility behavior and biological roles, not one polymer structure.
Steroids contain a characteristic fused-ring framework.|T|The common steroid nucleus has four fused rings.
Waxes are commonly esters of long-chain acids and long-chain alcohols.|T|Their long nonpolar portions contribute to water resistance.
Hydrogenating an unsaturated lipid decreases the number of carbon-carbon double bonds.|T|Hydrogen is added across the pi bonds, increasing saturation.
A nucleoside contains a nitrogenous base and a sugar.|T|Adding phosphate gives a nucleotide.
A nucleotide includes a phosphate group.|T|Its base-sugar-phosphate combination is a building block of nucleic acids.
DNA normally contains ribose rather than deoxyribose.|F|DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA normally contains ribose.
RNA normally uses uracil where DNA normally uses thymine.|T|Both can pair with adenine in their respective standard base-pairing contexts.
